The Western sand darter (Ammocrypta clara) is a small-bodied percid inhabiting sandy-bottomed streams across the central United States. Field surveys indicate that mature females attain a total length of 8.2 centimeters [Li = 8.2 centimeters], representing the ultimate size class observed in this species. Corresponding wet weight at the largest recorded individuals approaches 3.8 grams [Wwi = 3.8 grams], a mass that reflects the slender, fusiform body plan typical of sand-dwelling darters. In contrast, neonatal wet weight at the moment of hatching is considerably diminished; the tiny, yolk-dependent prolarvae emerge from adhesive demersal eggs at a mass of approximately 0.00052 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00052 grams]. This extremely low birth mass is consistent with the small egg diameter, roughly one millimeter, that characterizes the reproductive strategy of this species and many other members of the genus Ammocrypta.

Sexual maturation in female Western sand darters is attained at a standard length of 4.5 centimeters [Lp = 4.5 centimeters], a measurement that corresponds to the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the ability to produce viable oocytes. At this developmental milestone, the wet weight of a typical female reaches approximately 0.58 grams [Wwp = approximately 0.58 grams], a value derived from the robust length-mass scaling relationship established for the species. The shift from juvenile to adult physiology coincides with the initial accumulation of ovarian follicles and the emergence of secondary sexual characteristics, marking the transition to the reproductively viable stage of the life cycle. This pubertal length is slightly larger than that reported for the closely related congener Ammocrypta vivax, for which females reach maturity at a standard length of 3.9 centimeters, suggesting subtle interspecific variation in life-history scheduling within the group.

Reproductive output under optimal conditions has been characterized through controlled laboratory observations at a constant water temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C]. At this thermal regime, which approximates the summer maxima typical of the species' native range, individual females exhibit a maximum annual reproductive rate of 324 eggs per year [Ri = 324 eggs per year], one of the higher per-capita outputs documented among small-bodied darter species. The capacity to release eggs consistently across the reproductive period underscores the energetic investment that gravid females channel into gamete production, a strategy that balances high fecundity against the constraints of a relatively short adult lifespan.

Longevity data for the Western sand darter remain limited, but comparative studies drawing on the closely related eastern sand darter (Ammocrypta pellucida) provide a useful benchmark. At the same experimental temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], the maximum documented lifespan for the genus is estimated at 4 years [am = 4 years], from eclosion to death by senescence or post-reproductive mortality. This relatively compressed lifespan, typical of small, fast-living percids, aligns with an iteroparous reproductive schedule in which females invest heavily in repeated spawning bouts over two to three active seasons. The interplay between adult longevity and spawning frequency suggests that lifetime fecundity is maximized through steady, moderate annual egg production rather than a single, explosive reproductive event.

Habitat preferences of Ammocrypta clara are tightly linked to the presence of clean, shifting sand substrates in moderate- to high-velocity stream reaches, where the species buries itself with only the eyes and snout exposed. This cryptic behavior, combined with a protolarval stage that absorbs yolk nutrients before the onset of exogenous feeding, minimizes early mortality from visual predators. The transition from lecithotrophic to exotrophic nutrition occurs as the yolk-sac larva develops a functional mouth gape and completes retinal differentiation, at which point the juvenile begins to consume small benthic invertebrates such as chironomid larvae and microcrustaceans. Continued growth through the fingerling and sub-adult stages is supported by the high productivity of sandy stream habitats, although localized extirpations have been documented in systems impacted by siltation, channelization, or altered flow regimes that degrade the interstitial spaces essential for cover and foraging.
